config.editorData:
Host resources — is vSAN slow, or is the host out of road?

Every latency figure on every other screen is only meaningful if the host had capacity to spare. This screen answers that question first, so the others can be trusted.

Start with service health. A daemon that is not answering explains more than any latency number will. This pack can measure how much memory clomd and cmmdsd consume but has no way to tell whether they are responding, and vCenter checks exactly that, so the two halves are on the same screen deliberately.

CPU contention matters more than CPU usage. A host can be busy without anything waiting, and can make things wait while looking only moderately busy. Memory swap-in is the hard stop: any sustained non-zero value means memory was overcommitted far enough to page, and no latency figure anywhere else is reliable while it continues.

The physical CPU table is listed per CPU rather than per host, so a single hot core is visible instead of averaged away.

Host health and load

Renders the vSAN Host Uplinks and Load view.

Uplink RX Errors, All NICs — Inbound errors summed across every uplink on the host, counted by vCenter rather than by this pack. This pack only measures uplinks that carry vSAN traffic, which on this cluster is two of four per host, so a standby uplink going bad is invisible to it. This column is here to close that gap.

Uplink RX Dropped, All NICs — Inbound packets dropped across every uplink on the host.

Uplink TX Errors, All NICs — Outbound errors across every uplink on the host.

Uplink TX Dropped, All NICs — Outbound packets dropped across every uplink on the host.

Host Network Throughput — Total host network throughput, all uplinks and all traffic types. Context for the error columns and a check on whether vSAN is a large or a small share of what this host is doing.

Host CPU Usage — Host CPU usage from vCenter. On the screen so that vSAN latency can be read against host load: a saturated host produces vSAN latency that is not a vSAN problem.

Host CPU Contention — Proportion of time virtual machines waited for CPU. This, not usage, is the contention signal -- a host can be busy without anything waiting, and can make things wait while looking only moderately busy.

Host Memory Consumed — Proportion of host memory consumed.

Host Memory Swap-In Rate — Rate at which the host is reading memory back from disk. Any sustained non-zero value is serious: it means memory was overcommitted far enough to page, and every latency figure on every other panel becomes unreliable while it continues.

Host Uptime — Host uptime. Relevant here because many counters in this pack are cumulative since boot, so a recently rebooted host has small totals for reasons that have nothing to do with health.

Hardware Sensor Status — Overall hardware sensor health, as the host's own sensors report it. This replaced a set of vSAN daemon liveness columns that could not be displayed: those carry a current value but no retained history, and a view queries a time range, so every cell came back blank.

Connectivity Issues, Critical — Count of critical connectivity findings against this host. A tripwire rather than a diagnosis -- it tells you something is wrong and not what.

Utilisation Issues, Critical — Count of critical utilisation findings against this host.

vSAN daemon memory

Renders the vSAN Host Memory view.

Kernel consumed size — Memory the vSAN kernel modules are actually using. Measured at 2.14 GB against 21.0 GB reserved, so roughly a tenth of the reservation.

Kernel Reserved Memory Size — Memory reserved for the vSAN kernel modules. Reserved is not consumed -- compare the two columns rather than reading either alone.

Uw consumed size — Memory consumed by vSAN user-world processes in total.

User world Reserved Memory Size — Memory reserved for vSAN user-world processes.

Clomd consumed size — Memory used by clomd, which decides where objects and their replicas are placed. Growth here tracks object count, not IO.

Clomd reserved size — Memory reserved for clomd.

Cmmdsd consumed size — Memory used by cmmdsd, the cluster directory service that maintains membership and object metadata.

Cmmdsd reserved size — Memory reserved for cmmdsd.

Vsanmgmtd consumed size — Memory used by the vSAN management daemon, which answers the API calls this pack itself makes.

Epd consumed size — Memory used by epd, which handles object distribution.

Osfsd consumed size — Memory used by osfsd, the object filesystem daemon that presents vSAN objects as namespaces.

Vsandevicemonitord consumed size — Memory used by the device monitor, which watches disks for failure and degradation.

vSAN CPU - is it starved?

Renders the vSAN Host CPU view.

Percentage of Ready CPU Time — Time vSAN's own threads spent RUNNABLE but waiting for a physical CPU. This is the question the screen exists to answer: not whether the host is busy, but whether vSAN is being starved. A host can sit at modest utilisation and still show ready time if vSAN is losing the scheduler contest to guest workloads. Rising ready time with flat utilisation means contention, and it shows up as latency everywhere downstream before it shows up here.

Run percent (max) — The highest run percentage observed in the interval, across vSAN's threads. Read it next to the average: a high maximum with a modest average means bursty demand that the average hides, which is exactly the shape that produces intermittent latency nobody can reproduce.

Percentage of Used CPU Time — Physical CPU actually consumed by vSAN, as a share of one host's capacity. Capacity planning rather than diagnosis -- high is not itself a problem. Pair it with readyPct: high used with low ready is vSAN working hard and getting what it asks for; high ready is the one that hurts.

Percentage of Running CPU Time — Time vSAN's threads spent actually executing. Close to usedPct on a healthy host; a gap between them points at scheduling overhead rather than work.

Used percent (max) — Peak consumption in the interval. Useful for sizing headroom, and for telling a sustained load apart from a spike that an average would flatten away.
